title: On-Device Inference (Gemini Nano, ML Kit GenAI, MediaPipe)
scopeHtml: Scope: Running models on phones: what each stack offers, limits, privacy, fallbacks.

notes.title: What on-device inference is and why it exists
notes.html:
On-device inference means the language model runs on the phone itself: the prompt never leaves the device, and the tokens are produced by the phone's CPU, GPU or NPU (neural processing unit, a chip specialised for matrix math). Contrast this with the cloud pattern from the rest of this track, where the app sends a request to your backend, which calls a hosted model.

Four reasons teams do it:

  1. Privacy. Text such as messages, notes, health entries or voice transcripts is processed locally. No server log, no third-party processor, easier compliance reviews.
  2. Latency and availability. No network round trip (often 100 to 500 ms on mobile networks, much worse on bad ones), and it works in a tunnel or on a plane.
  3. Cost. Each request costs you zero inference dollars. The user pays with battery, heat and storage instead. At millions of daily users for tiny tasks (smart reply, summarising a notification) this is a real saving. See also 03_C1 notes (token economics) for how to price the cloud alternative.
  4. Product features that need to be instant, such as live keyboard suggestions.

The price: small models only. A phone has 6 to 16 GB of RAM shared with every other app, a thermal budget (the chip throttles when hot) and a battery. So on-device models are small (hundreds of millions to a few billion parameters), heavily quantized, and weaker than frontier cloud models. See also 02_Q1 notes (quantization, distillation) for how models are shrunk; this note focuses on how Android gives you access to them.

CLOUD                                   ON-DEVICE
app -> network -> your backend          app -> local runtime -> model file
    -> provider API -> big model            (CPU / GPU / NPU)
    <- tokens streamed back                 <- tokens, no network
cost: per token, paid by you            cost: battery + storage, paid by user
quality: frontier                       quality: small-model
privacy: data leaves device             privacy: data stays

Real products: Google Pixel features such as Recorder summaries and smart replies in Gboard use Gemini Nano; Samsung Galaxy AI mixes on-device and cloud; Apple Intelligence on iPhone (a different platform, but the same hybrid idea) runs a small on-device model and escalates harder requests to a server model.

Analogy (after the mechanism): the cloud is a head chef in a central kitchen who can cook anything but needs a delivery trip. On-device is the microwave in your own kitchen: instant and private, but it only does simple meals well.

Common interview traps.

  • "On-device is free": it moves cost to battery, storage, heat and engineering effort (device matrix, model delivery). It is not free.
  • "On-device replaces the cloud": no. Production apps use a hybrid with a fallback path, covered below.
  • Confusing on-device inference (running a model) with on-device training (rare; federated learning is a separate topic).

notes.title: The three stacks on Android: AICore, ML Kit GenAI, MediaPipe
notes.html:
There are three layers you will hear in interviews. Knowing which is which is the single most testable point.

Gemini Nano is the model, Google's smallest Gemini, built for phones. You do not ship it in your APK. It is managed by the system.

AICore is the Android system service that hosts Gemini Nano. It downloads and updates the model (via Google Play services / system updates), shares one copy between all apps (so ten apps do not each store a 2 GB file), schedules the NPU/GPU and applies safety filtering. Apps talk to AICore only through Google's SDKs. Availability is limited to supported devices (recent Pixel and some flagship phones from other makers; the list changes, verify on the current Android developer docs).

ML Kit GenAI APIs are the high-level, task-specific Kotlin/Java APIs on top of Gemini Nano via AICore. Instead of "give me a chat model", you get ready-made features: summarization, proofreading, rewriting, image description, and (newer, verify its stability label) a Prompt API for free-form prompts. Google tuned the model for each task using adapters, so quality for that narrow task is better than a generic small model with your hand-written prompt.

MediaPipe LLM Inference API (package com.google.mediapipe:tasks-genai) is the opposite end: a general runtime where YOU bring the model file (Gemma, Phi, Llama-family variants converted to a supported format) and run it. You own download, storage, updates and licence compliance. It works on far more devices than AICore, because it does not need Google's system model. Note: Google has been moving this line toward LiteRT-LM and the LiteRT runtime (the renamed TensorFlow Lite); check current docs before starting a new project (verify).

Your app
  |-- ML Kit GenAI (Summarizer, Rewriter, Prompt API)
  |        |
  |        v
  |     AICore (system service) --> Gemini Nano (shared, OS-managed)
  |
  |-- MediaPipe LLM Inference / LiteRT-LM
           |
           v
        your own model file (Gemma etc.) in app storage, run via CPU/GPU delegates
Question ML Kit GenAI (AICore) MediaPipe / LiteRT
Who supplies the model? Google (Gemini Nano) You (Gemma, etc.)
Model download OS-managed, shared Your app, your CDN
Device coverage Limited supported list Wide (needs enough RAM/GPU)
Control (prompt, sampling) Low to medium High
Fine-tuning / LoRA Not by you Yes (LoRA supported for some models)
Effort Lowest Highest

Analogy: ML Kit GenAI is ordering from the restaurant's menu. MediaPipe is renting the kitchen and cooking yourself.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "Gemini Nano ships inside my app": it does not; AICore manages it.
  • Treating ML Kit GenAI and MediaPipe as competitors with the same capability. One is a managed, task-based API, the other a bring-your-own-model runtime.
  • Forgetting that availability is per-device: you must always code a "not available" branch.

notes.title: ML Kit GenAI: task APIs and the feature lifecycle
notes.html:
Each ML Kit GenAI task follows the same four-step lifecycle. Understanding it matters more than memorising class names.

  1. Create a client for the task with options (for example summary style and language).
  2. Check feature status. Possible states are, in plain words: UNAVAILABLE (device cannot run it), DOWNLOADABLE (supported but the model/adapter is not yet present), DOWNLOADING, AVAILABLE (ready). Exact enum names: verify in the SDK docs.
  3. If DOWNLOADABLE, trigger the download and wait (may be hundreds of MB to a couple of GB, so show progress, prefer Wi-Fi).
  4. Run inference (blocking future or streaming callback), then close the client to free native resources.
checkFeatureStatus()
   |-- UNAVAILABLE ----> use cloud fallback / hide the feature
   |-- DOWNLOADABLE ---> downloadFeature() -> progress -> AVAILABLE
   |-- DOWNLOADING ----> wait (show spinner)
   '-- AVAILABLE ------> runInference() -> text (stream or whole)

The task APIs (names as of my knowledge; verify the exact artifacts and whether each is stable or beta):

  • Summarization: turns an article or chat into 1 to 3 bullets.
  • Proofreading: grammar and spelling fixes on short text.
  • Rewriting: change tone (friendly, formal, shorter, elaborate).
  • Image description: a short caption of an image (useful for accessibility).
  • Prompt API: send a free-form prompt (and, in some versions, an image) to Gemini Nano.

Input size is limited: the task APIs expect short inputs (on the order of a few thousand tokens at most; the exact limit is documented per API, verify). Feeding a 50-page document will fail or be truncated, so chunk it yourself.

Python (a desktop analogue of the lifecycle; there is no ML Kit in Python, so this shows the same decision logic with a local Ollama server plus cloud fallback):

import os, requests

def local_available() -> bool:
    try:
        return requests.get("http://localhost:11434/api/tags", timeout=0.5).ok  # Ollama up?
    except requests.RequestException:
        return False

def summarize(text: str) -> str:
    if local_available():
        r = requests.post("http://localhost:11434/api/generate", json={
            "model": "gemma3:1b", "prompt": f"Summarize in 3 bullets:\n{text}", "stream": False})
        return r.json()["response"]
    import anthropic  # fallback: cloud
    c = anthropic.Anthropic()  # key from ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
    m = c.messages.create(model="claude-haiku-5-5", max_tokens=200,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": f"Summarize in 3 bullets:\n{text}"}])
    return m.content[0].text   # prints: three bullet points

Kotlin (ML Kit GenAI Summarization; shape follows Google's docs, verify class and method names against the current SDK):

// build.gradle: implementation("com.google.mlkit:genai-summarization:<version>") // verify version
val options = SummarizerOptions.builder(context)
    .setInputType(SummarizerOptions.InputType.ARTICLE)
    .setOutputType(SummarizerOptions.OutputType.THREE_BULLETS)
    .setLanguage(SummarizerOptions.Language.ENGLISH)
    .build()
val summarizer = Summarization.getClient(options)

suspend fun summarize(text: String): String? {
    when (summarizer.checkFeatureStatus().await()) {
        FeatureStatus.UNAVAILABLE -> return null            // caller falls back to cloud
        FeatureStatus.DOWNLOADABLE -> summarizer.downloadFeature(/* callback */ null).await()
        else -> Unit                                         // AVAILABLE or DOWNLOADING
    }
    val request = SummarizationRequest.builder(text).build()
    return summarizer.runInference(request).await().summary  // returns: bullet text
}
// call summarizer.close() in onDestroy / when scope ends

Java (same API; callbacks via ListenableFuture):

Summarizer summarizer = Summarization.getClient(options); // options built as above
ListenableFuture<Integer> status = summarizer.checkFeatureStatus();
// After status == FeatureStatus.AVAILABLE:
SummarizationRequest req = SummarizationRequest.builder(text).build();
ListenableFuture<SummarizationResult> f = summarizer.runInference(req);
Futures.addCallback(f, new FutureCallback<SummarizationResult>() {
    @Override public void onSuccess(SummarizationResult r) { show(r.getSummary()); }
    @Override public void onFailure(Throwable t) { fallbackToCloud(); }
}, ContextCompat.getMainExecutor(context));
// summarizer.close() when finished

Analogy: it is like a phone's built-in camera app with a "portrait" mode: you do not tune the sensor, you just ask for the mode, and if the phone lacks it, the button is greyed out.

Common interview traps.

  • Calling inference without checking status first: crashes or exceptions on unsupported devices.
  • Triggering a large model download on mobile data without consent.
  • Passing huge inputs; these APIs are for short text.
  • Forgetting close(), which leaks native memory.

notes.title: MediaPipe LLM Inference: bring your own model
notes.html:
MediaPipe LLM Inference runs a model file stored on the device. The steps are:

  1. Choose a model small enough: Gemma 3 1B or Gemma 3n class models are typical examples (verify current names and licence terms; Gemma has its own licence you must accept).
  2. Convert or download the model in the format MediaPipe expects (a .task or .litertlm-style bundle, depending on version; verify).
  3. Deliver it to the device. Do NOT bundle it in the APK (APK/AAB size limits and a 1 GB model would wreck install rates). Download on first use into app-specific storage, verify a checksum, resume on failure.
  4. Create the engine with options (model path, max tokens, backend CPU or GPU, sampling settings).
  5. Call generate (blocking) or generateAsync (streaming partial results).

Memory math, shown step by step, because interviewers love it. Weights memory is parameters times bytes per parameter.

1B params  at 16-bit (2 bytes) = 1e9 * 2   = 2.0 GB
1B params  at  8-bit (1 byte)  = 1e9 * 1   = 1.0 GB
1B params  at  4-bit (0.5 B)   = 1e9 * 0.5 = 0.5 GB
3B params  at  4-bit           = 3e9 * 0.5 = 1.5 GB
Plus KV cache (grows with context) and runtime overhead.
KV cache per token = 2 (K and V) * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * bytes
   example (illustrative numbers, not a real model):
   2 * 26 layers * 4 kv_heads * 256 dim * 1 byte(int8) = 53,248 B ~ 52 KB/token
   4,096 tokens * 52 KB ~ 208 MB

So a 4-bit 1B model needs roughly 0.5 GB weights plus a few hundred MB of cache and overhead: fine on a 6 GB phone, risky on a 3 GB one. Android's low-memory killer terminates background apps first; a model of this size makes you the likely victim if the user switches apps.

Speed: decoding is memory-bandwidth bound (each new token reads all weights). Rough ceiling = memory bandwidth / model size. With 30 GB/s effective and 0.5 GB weights: 30 / 0.5 = 60 tokens/s theoretical; real phones deliver much less (often 10 to 30 tokens/s for 1B-class models; verify with your own benchmark on target devices, do not trust my range).

Python (MediaPipe has a Python package for desktop; verify package support for LLM tasks, so this also shows an equivalent llama-cpp approach):

# Desktop analogue of "bring your own model": llama-cpp-python with a 4-bit GGUF file.
from llama_cpp import Llama
llm = Llama(model_path="gemma-3-1b-it-Q4_K_M.gguf", n_ctx=2048, n_threads=4)
out = llm("Q: Name one use of on-device AI.\nA:", max_tokens=48)
print(out["choices"][0]["text"])  # prints: a short completion

Kotlin (MediaPipe tasks-genai; names per Google docs, verify against your version):

// implementation("com.google.mediapipe:tasks-genai:<version>")  // verify version
val opts = LlmInference.LlmInferenceOptions.builder()
    .setModelPath("${context.filesDir}/models/gemma3-1b-it-int4.task") // downloaded earlier
    .setMaxTokens(512)                   // prompt + response budget
    .setPreferredBackend(LlmInference.Backend.GPU) // or CPU; verify availability
    .build()
val llm = LlmInference.createFromOptions(context, opts)  // slow: seconds, do off main thread

val answer: String = llm.generateResponse("Explain DNS in one sentence.")
// Streaming variant: configure setResultListener { partial, done -> ... } then generateResponseAsync(prompt)
llm.close()  // free the model

Java:

LlmInference.LlmInferenceOptions opts = LlmInference.LlmInferenceOptions.builder()
    .setModelPath(context.getFilesDir() + "/models/gemma3-1b-it-int4.task")
    .setMaxTokens(512)
    .build();
LlmInference llm = LlmInference.createFromOptions(context, opts); // load on a background thread
String answer = llm.generateResponse("Explain DNS in one sentence."); // blocking call
llm.close();

Real tools: Google AI Edge Gallery (a sample app for trying on-device models), llama.cpp and MLC LLM (other runtimes with Android builds), Qualcomm and MediaTek vendor SDKs for NPU access.

Analogy: bringing your own model is buying a generator for the house instead of using the grid: more control, but you must store fuel, maintain it and live with the noise (heat).

Common interview traps.

  • Bundling the model in the APK/AAB.
  • Loading the model on the main thread (ANR: Application Not Responding, a freeze over about 5 s).
  • Ignoring that maxTokens covers prompt plus output.
  • Quoting tokens per second without naming the device, model size and quantization.

notes.title: Constraints: memory, thermals, battery, storage and context limits
notes.html:
On-device LLMs fail in practice for physical reasons, not API reasons.

Memory. Android kills processes under pressure (the low memory killer, lmkd). A 1.5 GB resident model makes your app a prime target when it goes to the background. Mitigations: load lazily, release the model in onTrimMemory (TRIM_MEMORY_BACKGROUND and up), keep the model inside a single owner object, never load two models at once.

Thermals. Sustained inference heats the SoC (system on a chip). The OS then lowers clock speeds ("thermal throttling"), so the first answer takes 3 s and the tenth takes 8 s. You can observe this with PowerManager.getCurrentThermalStatus() (API 29+) and listen for changes; back off or switch to cloud when status is SEVERE or worse.

Battery. An NPU is much more energy-efficient per token than the CPU, but still expensive compared with a network call for long outputs. Rule of thumb: short in, short out, run on user action, not continuously. Do not run background summarization of every notification on a 3,000 mAh battery.

Storage and download. Models are 0.5 to 4 GB. Use Play Asset Delivery or your own CDN; verify SHA-256; resume interrupted downloads; allow deletion in settings.

Context window. Small models support small windows in practice (a few thousand tokens), and the KV cache eats RAM as it grows. Long chats must be truncated or summarised. See also 01_I1 notes (KV-cache management) for the server-side view of the same problem.

Quality. A 1B to 4B model hallucinates more, follows complex instructions poorly and handles multi-step reasoning badly. Pick tasks that fit: classification, extraction, rewriting, short summaries, smart replies. Avoid open-ended factual Q&A and anything with legal or medical consequences.

Python (a tiny budget estimator you can run during design):

def fits(params_b: float, bits: int, ctx: int, kv_bytes_per_tok: int, ram_gb: float, headroom=0.35):
    weights = params_b * 1e9 * bits / 8
    kv = ctx * kv_bytes_per_tok
    need = weights + kv
    return need <= ram_gb * 1e9 * headroom   # leave room for OS and other apps
print(fits(1.0, 4, 4096, 53_000, 6))  # weights 0.5e9 + kv 0.217e9 = 0.717e9 <= 2.1e9 -> True

Kotlin (thermal and memory guards):

val pm = context.getSystemService(Context.POWER_SERVICE) as PowerManager
fun canRunLocally(): Boolean {
    if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 29 &&
        pm.currentThermalStatus >= PowerManager.THERMAL_STATUS_SEVERE) return false
    val mi = ActivityManager.MemoryInfo()
    (context.getSystemService(Context.ACTIVITY_SERVICE) as ActivityManager).getMemoryInfo(mi)
    return !mi.lowMemory && mi.availMem > 1_500_000_000L   // 1.5 GB free, tune per model
}

Java:

PowerManager pm = (PowerManager) context.getSystemService(Context.POWER_SERVICE);
ActivityManager.MemoryInfo mi = new ActivityManager.MemoryInfo();
((ActivityManager) context.getSystemService(Context.ACTIVITY_SERVICE)).getMemoryInfo(mi);
boolean hot = Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 29
        && pm.getCurrentThermalStatus() >= PowerManager.THERMAL_STATUS_SEVERE;
boolean ok = !hot && !mi.lowMemory && mi.availMem > 1_500_000_000L; // gate before loading the model

Analogy: a phone is a laptop in a sealed lunchbox with no fan. It can sprint but not run a marathon.

Common interview traps.

  • Benchmarking on a cold, charged flagship and shipping to all devices.
  • Ignoring thermal status.
  • Choosing an on-device model for tasks needing broad world knowledge.
  • Forgetting to release the model on onTrimMemory.

notes.title: Privacy and security reality check
notes.html:
"On-device" is a strong privacy story but not a magic one.

What you genuinely gain: prompts and outputs stay in process memory; no third-party processor; works offline; good for GDPR/health-data minimisation arguments. AICore adds a design where the model service is isolated and Google states that inference data is not sent to Google for these features (verify the current privacy documentation before promising this to a client).

What you must still handle:

  • Logs. Do not log prompts with Log.d or ship them to Crashlytics. On-device privacy is lost the moment your analytics SDK uploads the text.
  • Model file integrity. If you download a model, verify a hash and signature; a swapped model file is a supply-chain attack. Store it in app-private storage (filesDir), not shared external storage.
  • Prompt injection still exists. If the model summarises a web page or email containing "ignore previous instructions", a small local model is even easier to fool than a big one. Treat its output as untrusted text; never let it trigger actions (send, delete, pay) without user confirmation. See also the safety notes in the C2 track for guardrail patterns.
  • Fallback leakage. A hybrid app that silently sends text to the cloud when the local model is unavailable breaks the privacy promise. Make the fallback explicit: ask consent, or restrict sensitive categories to local-only and show "not available on this device".
  • Content safety. AICore applies safety filters; with MediaPipe you must add your own (blocklist, classifier, or a second small model).
  • Rooted devices and memory dumps: on-device data is only as safe as the device. Do not claim "unreadable".

Python (policy gate deciding where a request may run):

SENSITIVE = {"health", "finance", "messages"}
def route(category: str, local_ok: bool, user_consented_cloud: bool) -> str:
    if local_ok:
        return "local"
    if category in SENSITIVE:
        return "refuse"          # never auto-fallback for sensitive data
    return "cloud" if user_consented_cloud else "ask_consent"
print(route("health", False, True))  # prints: refuse

Kotlin:

enum class Route { LOCAL, CLOUD, ASK_CONSENT, REFUSE }
fun route(category: String, localOk: Boolean, consented: Boolean): Route = when {
    localOk -> Route.LOCAL
    category in setOf("health", "finance", "messages") -> Route.REFUSE
    consented -> Route.CLOUD
    else -> Route.ASK_CONSENT
}

Java:

enum Route { LOCAL, CLOUD, ASK_CONSENT, REFUSE }
static Route route(String category, boolean localOk, boolean consented) {
    if (localOk) return Route.LOCAL;
    if (Set.of("health", "finance", "messages").contains(category)) return Route.REFUSE;
    return consented ? Route.CLOUD : Route.ASK_CONSENT;
}

Analogy: on-device AI is a diary kept in your own room. Private, unless you photocopy pages for the cloud "just in case" or leave the diary open on the desk (logs).

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming "100% private" while logging prompts or auto-falling back to a cloud API.
  • Not verifying downloaded model checksums.
  • Assuming a local model is safer against prompt injection.

notes.title: Fallbacks and the hybrid architecture
notes.html:
Every real app needs a decision layer that picks where each request runs. Triggers for leaving the local path:

  • Device unsupported (status UNAVAILABLE) or model not yet downloaded and the user cannot wait.
  • Input too long for the local context window.
  • Task too hard (needs reasoning, tools, retrieval over big data).
  • Thermal or memory guard trips.
  • Local call fails or exceeds a latency deadline (say 3 s to first token).
request
  |
  v
[policy] sensitive? -----yes----> local only (else refuse)
  | no
  v
local available AND input fits AND device healthy?
  |yes                         |no
  v                            v
run local ---fail/timeout--->  cloud via YOUR backend proxy
  |                            (never a raw provider key in the APK)
  v
stream result to UI; record which route ran (no prompt text) for metrics

Important design points:

  1. The cloud path goes through your own backend, which holds the API key (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY as an environment variable server-side), enforces quotas and rate limits, and can call claude-haiku-5-5 or claude-sonnet-5-5 (verify model ids). See also 07_K notes and 03_C1 notes for proxy and cost control patterns.
  2. Keep one interface, TextGenerator, with two implementations (Local, Cloud) so UI and tests do not care. A third Fake implementation makes tests deterministic.
  3. Race or cascade? Cascade (try local, fall back) is cheaper; racing both wastes cost. Use a deadline on the local attempt.
  4. Quality routing: use local for easy tasks, send hard ones to cloud. A tiny classifier or simple rules (length, keyword, task type) is enough to start.
  5. Metrics: route taken, time to first token, fallback reason, thermal state, device model. Never log the text.
  6. Streaming parity: both paths should stream tokens so the UI code is identical.

Python (cascade with deadline):

import concurrent.futures as cf
def generate(prompt, local_fn, cloud_fn, deadline_s=3.0):
    with cf.ThreadPoolExecutor(1) as ex:
        fut = ex.submit(local_fn, prompt)
        try:
            return "local", fut.result(timeout=deadline_s)
        except Exception:               # timeout or local failure
            return "cloud", cloud_fn(prompt)

Kotlin:

interface TextGenerator { suspend fun generate(prompt: String): String }

class HybridGenerator(
    private val local: TextGenerator?, private val cloud: TextGenerator,
) : TextGenerator {
    override suspend fun generate(prompt: String): String =
        try {
            withTimeout(3_000) { local?.generate(prompt) ?: error("no local") }
        } catch (e: Exception) {            // timeout, unavailable, runtime error
            cloud.generate(prompt)          // cloud = HTTP call to your backend proxy
        }
}

Java:

interface TextGenerator { CompletableFuture<String> generate(String prompt); }

class HybridGenerator implements TextGenerator {
    private final TextGenerator local; private final TextGenerator cloud; // local may be null
    HybridGenerator(TextGenerator l, TextGenerator c) { local = l; cloud = c; }
    public CompletableFuture<String> generate(String prompt) {
        if (local == null) return cloud.generate(prompt);
        return local.generate(prompt)
            .orTimeout(3, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
            .exceptionallyCompose(t -> cloud.generate(prompt)); // fall back on any failure
    }
}

Real examples: Google Messages and Gboard (local for suggestions), Samsung Galaxy AI (some features marked as cloud and require sign-in, others local), Apple Intelligence (on-device with escalation to Private Cloud Compute). The common lesson: the user-visible label says where processing happens.

Analogy: a hospital triage desk. The nurse (local) handles minor cases instantly and sends complex cases to the specialist (cloud).

Common interview traps.

  • Putting provider API keys in the app as the "fallback".
  • Using fallback silently for sensitive data.
  • No timeout on the local path, so a stuck NPU hangs the UI.
  • Different output formats between the two paths breaking parsing.

notes.title: Model delivery, updates and device fragmentation
notes.html:
Android has thousands of device models. Your test matrix is the hard part.

Fragmentation facts.

  • AICore/Gemini Nano support is limited to certain chipsets and OS versions; capability differs per device (verify the supported-devices page).
  • MediaPipe on CPU works broadly but slowly; GPU delegates vary by driver quality; NPU access is vendor-specific (Qualcomm, MediaTek, Samsung, Google Tensor).
  • RAM tiers matter more than CPU: gate by ActivityManager.getMemoryInfo().totalMem and by isLowRamDevice.

Capability tiers (a practical approach).

Tier A: >= 8 GB RAM, supported by AICore  -> Gemini Nano via ML Kit GenAI
Tier B: >= 6 GB RAM, no AICore            -> MediaPipe + 1B-class 4-bit model, GPU if stable
Tier C: < 6 GB or low-RAM flag            -> cloud only (or feature hidden)

These thresholds are examples; derive yours from benchmarks on your lowest supported phone.

Delivery. Options: Play Asset Delivery (on-demand asset packs; there are size limits per pack and total, verify the current numbers), your own CDN with HTTP range requests for resume, or Firebase ML custom model hosting for smaller models. Always: checksum, version field, atomic rename (download to .tmp, verify, then move), delete old versions, and respect Data Saver and metered networks (use WorkManager with NetworkType.UNMETERED and setRequiresStorageNotLow).

Updates. Model versions change output behaviour. Pin the model version in remote config; roll out by percentage; keep an A/B flag so you can revert. With AICore, Google updates Nano silently, so your prompts can change behaviour without an app release. Keep regression tests (golden prompts with tolerance checks, not exact string matches) and run them on a device farm (Firebase Test Lab, Samsung Remote Test Lab).

Python (server-side manifest your app polls; chooses model by device tier):

MANIFEST = {
  "B": {"url": "https://cdn.example.com/gemma3-1b-int4-v3.task", "sha256": "<hex>", "size": 555_000_000},
}
def pick(tier: str):
    return MANIFEST.get(tier)   # None -> client uses cloud only
print(pick("C"))  # prints: None

Kotlin (WorkManager constraints for the download):

val request = OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<ModelDownloadWorker>()
    .setConstraints(Constraints.Builder()
        .setRequiredNetworkType(NetworkType.UNMETERED)  // Wi-Fi only by default
        .setRequiresStorageNotLow(true)
        .setRequiresBatteryNotLow(true)
        .build())
    .build()
WorkManager.getInstance(context).enqueueUniqueWork("model", ExistingWorkPolicy.KEEP, request)

Java:

Constraints c = new Constraints.Builder()
        .setRequiredNetworkType(NetworkType.UNMETERED)
        .setRequiresStorageNotLow(true)
        .setRequiresBatteryNotLow(true)
        .build();
OneTimeWorkRequest req = new OneTimeWorkRequest.Builder(ModelDownloadWorker.class)
        .setConstraints(c).build();
WorkManager.getInstance(context).enqueueUniqueWork("model", ExistingWorkPolicy.KEEP, req);

Analogy: shipping a model is like selling a cooking appliance across a thousand kitchen layouts: you need sizing tiers, a manual per tier and a return policy.

Common interview traps.

  • Testing on two Pixel phones and calling it done.
  • Forgetting that AICore updates can change behaviour without your release.
  • Downloading over metered networks without asking.
  • Non-atomic downloads leaving a corrupt half-model that crashes on load.

notes.title: Prompting and quality techniques for small models
notes.html:
Small models behave differently from frontier ones. Techniques that work (see also 02_Q1 notes for why the model is small):

  1. Be explicit and short. Long, nuanced system prompts get partly ignored. Put the task first, then the input, then the output format.
  2. Constrain the output. Ask for one of N labels, or JSON with 2 to 3 fields, and validate it in code. Retry once, then fall back.
  3. Few-shot examples help more than rules: two short examples of input and output beat a paragraph of instructions.
  4. Lower temperature (0.0 to 0.4) for extraction and classification; small models drift at high temperature.
  5. Use grammar-constrained or schema-constrained decoding if the runtime supports it (llama.cpp has grammars; verify MediaPipe support).
  6. Cap maxTokens. Cutting generation early saves battery and latency.
  7. Chunk long inputs. Summarise sections, then summarise the summaries.
  8. Evaluate on your own device set with a golden test set of 50 to 200 prompts, scoring with simple checks (label match, JSON validity, length). Use a cloud model as an offline judge, not at runtime.

LoRA adapters (small add-on weights, a few MB to tens of MB) can specialise a base model for your task without shipping a whole new model. MediaPipe supports LoRA for some Gemma variants (verify the supported list); ML Kit GenAI uses Google-trained adapters internally, which you cannot replace.

Python (classification with validation and retry):

import json
LABELS = {"billing", "bug", "feature", "other"}
def classify(llm, text):
    p = ('Classify the message. Reply JSON only: {"label": one of billing|bug|feature|other}\n'
         'Message: ' + text)
    for _ in range(2):                       # retry once
        try:
            label = json.loads(llm(p))["label"]
            if label in LABELS: return label
        except (ValueError, KeyError, TypeError):
            pass
    return "other"                           # safe default

Kotlin:

private val labels = setOf("billing", "bug", "feature", "other")
suspend fun classify(gen: TextGenerator, text: String): String {
    val prompt = "Classify the message. Reply with exactly one word: billing, bug, feature or other.\nMessage: $text"
    repeat(2) {
        val out = gen.generate(prompt).trim().lowercase()
        if (out in labels) return out
    }
    return "other"
}

Java:

static final Set<String> LABELS = Set.of("billing", "bug", "feature", "other");
String classify(TextGenerator gen, String text) throws Exception {
    String prompt = "Classify the message. Reply with exactly one word: billing, bug, feature or other.\nMessage: " + text;
    for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) {
        String out = gen.generate(prompt).get().trim().toLowerCase();
        if (LABELS.contains(out)) return out;
    }
    return "other";
}

Analogy: a small model is a bright intern on day one. Give it a checklist and examples, not an essay, and check its work before it goes to the customer.

Common interview traps.

  • Porting a 2,000-token cloud prompt unchanged.
  • Trusting free-form output without validation.
  • Judging quality on five hand-picked prompts.
  • Setting high temperature for structured tasks.

notes.title: Production failure patterns and monitoring
notes.html:
Patterns seen when teams ship on-device GenAI (some are my synthesis of common mobile issues, not published statistics):

Symptom Likely cause Fix
ANR on first use Model loaded on main thread Load on Dispatchers.Default/executor, show progress
OOM kill, "app restarted" reports Model plus UI memory exceeds limit Smaller quantization, unload on onTrimMemory, lower context
First answer slow, later faster (or reverse) Warm-up and compilation vs thermal throttle Warm up on idle, monitor thermal status
Feature works on Pixel, absent elsewhere AICore not supported Status check, hide or fall back
Corrupt model crash at load Interrupted download Checksum plus atomic rename
Output changed after weeks Silent Nano update Pin where possible, golden tests, flag-based fallback
Battery complaints Continuous background inference Run on user action only, batch work in WorkManager when charging
Users on cellular charged for data Auto download on metered network Unmetered constraint, consent dialog

Metrics worth tracking (never raw prompts): feature status distribution by device model, time to first token (p50 and p95), tokens per second, fallback rate and reason, crash-free rate in sessions that used the model, download success rate, thermal state at start, thumbs-up/down rate.

Rollout: ship behind a remote flag; start at 1 percent on Tier A devices; watch crash rate and fallback rate; expand. Keep a kill switch that turns the feature off or forces cloud-only without an app release.

Python (aggregating metrics server-side to find the worst device models):

from collections import defaultdict
def fallback_rate_by_device(events):
    tot, fb = defaultdict(int), defaultdict(int)
    for e in events:                          # e = {"device": str, "route": "local"|"cloud", "reason": str|None}
        tot[e["device"]] += 1
        fb[e["device"]] += e["route"] == "cloud"
    return {d: fb[d] / tot[d] for d in tot}   # e.g. {"Pixel 9": 0.02, "Galaxy A15": 0.91}

Kotlin (timing first token):

suspend fun timed(gen: TextGenerator, prompt: String): Pair<String, Long> {
    val t0 = SystemClock.elapsedRealtime()
    val out = gen.generate(prompt)
    return out to (SystemClock.elapsedRealtime() - t0)   // send duration + device model, not the text
}

Java:

long t0 = SystemClock.elapsedRealtime();
String out = gen.generate(prompt).get();
long ms = SystemClock.elapsedRealtime() - t0;
analytics.log("genai_latency", Map.of("ms", ms, "device", Build.MODEL)); // no prompt text

Analogy: shipping on-device AI without monitoring is like opening a restaurant chain where each branch has a different oven and never reading the complaint cards.

Common interview traps.

  • Reporting average latency instead of p95.
  • No kill switch.
  • Logging prompts in analytics.
  • Measuring only success and not fallback rate.

notes.title: Choosing: on-device, cloud or hybrid (decision guide)
notes.html:
A short checklist to answer "should we run this on-device?" in an interview.

  1. Data sensitivity: highly personal or regulated, and users expect it stays local? Lean on-device.
  2. Task difficulty: classification, extraction, rewriting, short summaries? On-device is fine. Multi-step reasoning, tool use, long documents, broad knowledge? Cloud.
  3. Latency target: instant keyboard-level (under 300 ms)? On-device. Seconds are acceptable? Either.
  4. Connectivity: offline use cases (field work, travel)? On-device needed.
  5. Scale and cost: millions of cheap calls a day? On-device saves money. Rare, high-value calls? Cloud cost is trivial.
  6. Device reach: if you must support low-end phones, you need the cloud path regardless.
  7. Team capacity: ML Kit GenAI is cheap to adopt; MediaPipe needs model ops (delivery, evaluation, licence, safety).

Cost sanity check with shown math. Suppose 1M daily users, 5 smart-reply calls each, 300 input plus 20 output tokens. That is 1e6 x 5 = 5e6 calls/day, x 320 tokens = 1.6e9 tokens/day. At a hypothetical cloud price of 0.25 dollars per million input tokens and 1.25 dollars per million output tokens (made-up numbers, verify real prices): input 5e6 x 300 = 1.5e9 tokens = 1,500 x 0.25 = 375 dollars/day; output 5e6 x 20 = 1e8 tokens = 100 x 1.25 = 125 dollars/day; total 500 dollars/day, about 15,000 per month. On-device removes that, but costs engineering plus support on a device matrix. The break-even depends on your volume; at 10,000 daily users the same math gives 5 dollars/day and cloud wins easily.

Python (decision function for design discussions):

def where(sensitive, hard, offline, low_end_device):
    if low_end_device: return "cloud"
    if hard: return "cloud"
    if sensitive or offline: return "on-device"
    return "hybrid"
print(where(True, False, False, False))  # prints: on-device

Kotlin:

fun where(sensitive: Boolean, hard: Boolean, offline: Boolean, lowEnd: Boolean) = when {
    lowEnd || hard -> "cloud"
    sensitive || offline -> "on-device"
    else -> "hybrid"
}

Java:

static String where(boolean sensitive, boolean hard, boolean offline, boolean lowEnd) {
    if (lowEnd || hard) return "cloud";
    if (sensitive || offline) return "on-device";
    return "hybrid";
}

Analogy: you do not hire an architect to hang a picture frame, and you do not hang a picture frame to build a skyscraper. Match the tool to the job.

Common interview traps.

  • Answering "on-device, because privacy" without considering task difficulty and device reach.
  • Ignoring the cloud path for low-end devices.
  • Comparing cloud cost to zero instead of to engineering and support cost.
  • Forgetting offline as the strongest argument for local.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• On-device inference runs a small, quantized model on the phone: private, fast to start, offline, no per-token cost, but limited by RAM, heat, battery, storage and model quality.
  • Gemini Nano is the model; AICore is the system service that hosts and updates it; ML Kit GenAI gives task APIs (summarize, proofread, rewrite, image description, Prompt API) over it; MediaPipe LLM Inference (and the LiteRT-LM direction, verify) runs a model file you supply.
  • The ML Kit lifecycle is: client, check status, download if needed, run, close. Always code the UNAVAILABLE branch.
  • Weights memory = parameters x bytes per parameter (1B at 4-bit is about 0.5 GB); add KV cache and overhead; decoding speed is bounded by memory bandwidth.
  • Guard against thermal throttling, low memory and metered networks; deliver models by download with checksums and atomic writes, never inside the APK.
  • Privacy needs discipline: no prompt logging, no silent cloud fallback for sensitive data, verified model files, and untrusted output handling.
  • Build a hybrid: one TextGenerator interface, local first with a deadline, cloud via your own backend proxy, metrics without prompt text, a kill switch.
  • Small models need short prompts, constrained outputs, validation and a golden test set.
  • Decide by sensitivity, task difficulty, latency, connectivity, scale and device reach, and always show the cost math.
  • Unverified and fast-moving: exact ML Kit class and enum names, artifact versions, supported device lists, input limits, MediaPipe vs LiteRT-LM status, Gemma model names and licences, example prices.
